questions.q: Professor Majida Asad overcame many obstacles to her education and career. What does she advise when facing disagreement?
options: Avoid stating your view at all
Not quite. The article says: Speak in a soft tone and present your case with full conviction – truthfulness wins over an opponent.
Speak in a soft tone and present your case with full conviction – truthfulness wins over an opponent
Yes. Gentleness with firmness.
Leave the discussion at once
Not quite. The article says: Speak in a soft tone and present your case with full conviction – truthfulness wins over an opponent.
Raise your voice so as to be heard
Not quite. The article says: Speak in a soft tone and present your case with full conviction – truthfulness wins over an opponent.
questions.rationale: “To tackle any situation of disagreement and confrontation, she advises one to speak in a soft tone, present one’s arguments with complete conviction.”

questions.q: Why does the article say pride is never a harmless feeling of self-respect?
options: Pride is comparative – it carries the thought “I am better than others,” and grows into arrogance
Well reasoned. The very words attributed to Satan.
Because others quickly notice it
Not quite. The article says: Pride is comparative – it carries the thought “I am better than others,” and grows into arrogance.
Because it is tiring to maintain
Not quite. The article says: Pride is comparative – it carries the thought “I am better than others,” and grows into arrogance.
Because it makes people work too hard
Not quite. The article says: Pride is comparative – it carries the thought “I am better than others,” and grows into arrogance.
questions.rationale: “Being ‘proud’ is a comparative adjective. Pride always arises in comparison to someone else… there is a feeling that ‘I am better than others.’”

questions.q: What does the article say is the only difference between pride and arrogance?
options: Pride is private; arrogance is public
Not quite. The article says: The spelling – in reality they are the same.
Pride is brief; arrogance is lasting
Not quite. The article says: The spelling – in reality they are the same.
Pride is earned; arrogance is not
Not quite. The article says: The spelling – in reality they are the same.
The spelling – in reality they are the same
Right. One becomes the other.
questions.rationale: “The only difference between pride and arrogance is that of spelling. In reality, there is no difference between the two.”

questions.q: Which three values does the article say fasting in Ramadan is meant to build?
options: Thrift, caution and silence
Not quite. The article says: Consciousness of God (taqwa), thankfulness (shukr) and patience (sabr).
Consciousness of God (taqwa), thankfulness (shukr) and patience (sabr)
Yes. From the Quran and the Hadith.
Strength, speed and endurance
Not quite. The article says: Consciousness of God (taqwa), thankfulness (shukr) and patience (sabr).
Knowledge, eloquence and memory
Not quite. The article says: Consciousness of God (taqwa), thankfulness (shukr) and patience (sabr).
questions.rationale: “So the three values mentioned in the Quran and Hadiths are Fear of God, Thanksgiving and Patience.”

questions.q: How does going without food and water lead to thankfulness, according to the article?
options: One is praised by others for fasting
Not quite. The article says: One feels how essential these gifts are, and realises that all one enjoys comes from God.
One feels how essential these gifts are, and realises that all one enjoys comes from God
Well read. Felt most keenly at the breaking of the fast.
One eats better food in the evening
Not quite. The article says: One feels how essential these gifts are, and realises that all one enjoys comes from God.
One saves money during the month
Not quite. The article says: One feels how essential these gifts are, and realises that all one enjoys comes from God.
questions.rationale: “When you observe fasting, you experience the true value of food and water… one starts feeling that all things that we enjoy are gifts of God.”

questions.q: Why does the article hold that an ideal person is possible in this world but an ideal society is not?
options: A person can reform himself by his own will, but everyone is free, and some will always misuse that freedom
Correct. So the individual, not society, is the target.
Ideal people refuse to live together
Not quite. The article says: A person can reform himself by his own will, but everyone is free, and some will always misuse that freedom.
Societies are too large to count
Not quite. The article says: A person can reform himself by his own will, but everyone is free, and some will always misuse that freedom.
Laws are always badly written
Not quite. The article says: A person can reform himself by his own will, but everyone is free, and some will always misuse that freedom.
questions.rationale: “Freedom means having more than one option. Because of this option, it will always be the case that some people will use freedom properly and some people will abuse it.”

questions.q: The article describes two ways of living. What are they?
options: A life of learning and a life of trade
Not quite. The article says: A life led by desire – anger, envy, greed – and a life led by principle – honesty, humility, forgiveness.
A life in the city and a life in the village
Not quite. The article says: A life led by desire – anger, envy, greed – and a life led by principle – honesty, humility, forgiveness.
A life of work and a life of leisure
Not quite. The article says: A life led by desire – anger, envy, greed – and a life led by principle – honesty, humility, forgiveness.
A life led by desire – anger, envy, greed – and a life led by principle – honesty, humility, forgiveness
Right. Only the second is fully human.
questions.rationale: “The life of every human being lies between two contradictory requirements: desire and principles.”

questions.q: Which of these does the article list among the marks of a principled person?
options: He speaks more than he listens
Not quite. The article says: He keeps his promises, is free of double standards, and knows how to acknowledge others.
He always gets his own way
Not quite. The article says: He keeps his promises, is free of double standards, and knows how to acknowledge others.
He keeps his promises, is free of double standards, and knows how to acknowledge others
Yes. And to forgive.
He never admits a mistake
Not quite. The article says: He keeps his promises, is free of double standards, and knows how to acknowledge others.
questions.rationale: “A principled person knows how to love others, who keeps his promises… who is free from double standards, who is humble, who knows how to acknowledge others.”

questions.q: What effect of anger, reported in a study the article cites, makes it unwise to act while angry?
options: It makes us forget what happened
Not quite. The article says: It makes us more impulsive and leads us to underestimate the chance of a bad outcome.
It improves our judgement of risk
Not quite. The article says: It makes us more impulsive and leads us to underestimate the chance of a bad outcome.
It makes us too cautious to act
Not quite. The article says: It makes us more impulsive and leads us to underestimate the chance of a bad outcome.
It makes us more impulsive and leads us to underestimate the chance of a bad outcome
Exactly. Hence the advice to stay quiet until calm.
questions.rationale: “Feeling anger can alter the way we view risks. Studies have shown that it can make us more impulsive and make us underestimate the chances of bad outcomes.”

questions.q: “If God were to grant abundant provision to all His creatures, they would act insolently on earth” (42:27). What does the commentary draw from this?
options: Effort has no bearing on provision
Not quite. The article says: Provision is given in due measure, with knowledge of what each person can bear without becoming arrogant.
Wealth is always a punishment
Not quite. The article says: Provision is given in due measure, with knowledge of what each person can bear without becoming arrogant.
Provision is given in due measure, with knowledge of what each person can bear without becoming arrogant
Well read. Excess can corrupt.
The poor are dearer to God than the rich
Not quite. The article says: Provision is given in due measure, with knowledge of what each person can bear without becoming arrogant.
questions.rationale: “If people are given greater abundance than they can deal with equanimity, they will become obstreperous and arrogant.”
